claims.claim: To mark Axelrod's 20th anniversary, the two tournaments were recreated at the 2004 IEEE Congress on Evolutionary Computation (CEC'04) and the 2005 IEEE Symposium on Computational Intelligence and Games (CIG'05). The rules changed in two ways: noise (moves mis-executed with small probability) was added, and entrants were explicitly invited to submit more than one player.
claims.quote: To stimulate novel research, the rules of Axelrod's original tournaments were extended in two key ways. Firstly, noise was introduced, whereby the moves of each player would be mis-executed with some small probability. Secondly, researchers were explicitly invited to enter more than one player into the round-robin style tournament.
claims.source_title: Rogers, Dash, Ramchurn, Vytelingum, Jennings, 'Coordinating team players within a noisy Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma tournament', Theoretical Computer Science 377 (2007) 243-259
claims.notes: This was written by the Southampton team themselves, not the organizers. The organizers' own chapter (Chong, Humble, Kendall, Li, Yao, ch.1 of '20 Years On', DOI 10.1142/9789812770684_0001) returned 403 and was not read. Slany & Kienreich name the organizers as 'Graham Kendall, Paul Darwen and Xin Yao'. The book's editors were Kendall, Yao and Chong.

claims.claim: The Southampton team was Nick Jennings, Alex Rogers, Gopal (Sarvapali D.) Ramchurn, Raj (Rajdeep K.) Dash and Krishnen (Perukrishnen) Vytelingum. The university announced the win on 7 October 2004.
claims.source_title: University of Southampton news: 'team wins competition' (7 Oct 2004)
claims.notes: The press release lists five names, the same as the TCS paper's authors (A. Rogers, R.K. Dash, S.D. Ramchurn, P. Vytelingum, N.R. Jennings). The tool would not reproduce the full release text. It gives no entry count, no strategy count and no rankings. It says the team won the '20th anniversary challenge' in a noisy environment and that the method uses coding theory.

claims.claim: Wired (Wendy M. Grossman, 13 Oct 2004): the 2004 competition had 223 entries, Southampton submitted 60 programs, and Southampton had the top three performers.
claims.quote: the Southampton team submitted 60 programs
claims.source_title: Wired, 'New Tack Wins Prisoner's Dilemma' (repost; original wired.com/2004/10/new-tack-wins-prisoners-dilemma/)
claims.notes: wired.com refused the fetch, so this was read from a repost that credits Wired. The figure '60 programs' conflicts with the papers: Rogers et al. 2007 say 4 teams x 28 = 112, and Slany & Kienreich say the STAR group had 112 members. See M06/M07. Other quotes from the repost: 'The 2004 competition had 223 entries'; 'Southampton had the top three performers'.

claims.claim: Wired describes recognition as 'a known series of five to 10 moves'. After recognition the programs took 'master and slave' roles: one sacrificed itself so the other could win repeatedly. The sacrificing programs ended near the bottom of the table.
claims.quote: a load of utter failures at the bottom of the table who sacrificed themselves for the good of the team
claims.source_title: Wired, 'New Tack Wins Prisoner's Dilemma' (repost)
claims.notes: Wired gives no exact count of how many Southampton programs finished at the bottom. The Rogers paper describes the code word as a fixed-length binary sequence of opening moves, tested at 1-16 bits, with an optimum length. The competition entries used a Hamming code in 2004 and a [15,5] BCH code in 2005, so the 2005 code word was 15 moves. That is longer than the 'five to 10' in Wired.

claims.claim: Wired attributes the 'around 20' remark to organizer Graham Kendall, not to Southampton: 'It turns out we had far too many — we would have won with around 20.'
claims.quote: It turns out we had far too many — we would have won with around 20.
claims.source_title: Wired, 'New Tack Wins Prisoner's Dilemma' (repost)
claims.notes: Attribution caveat: the WebFetch reader assigned this to Kendall from the 'he said' context. The pronoun 'we' reads oddly for an organizer, so check against the original Wired text before quoting. The same article says Kendall planned a second competition for April 2005.

claims.claim: Primary source, Southampton's own account: entries were unlimited in 2004, so they entered four teams of 28 players each, all using a single-block Hamming code. Their team leader, with TFT as its default strategy, won by 13% over the second-placed competing player.
claims.quote: In the first competition there was no limit on the number of players that could be submitted, and thus, we entered four different teams. Each team consisted of 28 players, and used the single block Hamming code for recognition. ... the team leader that employed tit-for-tat as a default strategy won the competition by a significant margin (it scored 13% more than the second placed competing player).
claims.source_title: Rogers et al., Theoretical Computer Science 377 (2007) 243-259
claims.notes: 4 x 28 = 112 players, which contradicts Wired's '60'. The paper does not say which 2004 league (noise-free or noisy) the 13% refers to. It does not match Slany's league-1 table (M08): StarSN 117,057 vs GRIM 100,611 is +16.3%, and vs teammate StarS 110,611 is +5.8%. 'Competing player' probably means non-team, but 13% still does not fit league 1, so it may refer to the noisy league. The book-chapter version (ch.9 of '20 Years On', 2006 preprint) says instead: 'the team leader from the largest team won with a clear advantage', with no numbers.

claims.claim: Slany & Kienreich, a rival team, describe the 2004 league 1 as standard IPD rules with 223 strategies. The winning 'STAR' group sent in by Gopal Ramchurn had 112 members, just over half the field.
claims.quote: after the STAR group strategy of Gopal Ramchurn (with 112 members, though we are not sure that all strategies colluded as one group). ... 112 is exactly the smallest integer larger than 223 divided by 2, so the STAR group members were just more than 50% of the total population.
claims.source_title: Slany & Kienreich, 'On some winning strategies for the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma or Mr. Nice Guy and the Cosa Nostra' (arXiv 2006; ch.8 of '20 Years On', 2007, pp.171-204)
claims.notes: This independently confirms 112, not 60. It is a competitor's account. They also complain that their own 10,000+ clone 'EmperorAndHisClones' entry was cut to a single copy.

claims.claim: 2004 league 1 top 10 (Slany Table 8.1a): StarSN 117,057, StarS 110,611 and StarSL 110,511 (all Ramchurn/Southampton) took 1st-3rd. Next came GRIM 100,611 (4th) and OmegaTFT 100,604 (5th). Plain TFT is not in the top 10.
claims.quote: 1 Gopal Ramchurn StarSN (StarSN) 117,057 / 2 Gopal Ramchurn StarS (StarS) 110,611 / 3 Gopal Ramchurn StarSL (StarSL) 110,511 / 4 GRIM (GRIM Trigger)_1 GRIM (GRIM Trigger) 100,611 / 5 Wolfgang Kienreich OTFT (Omega tit for tat) 100,604
claims.source_title: Slany & Kienreich (2006/2007), Table 8.1a 'Original tournament results'
claims.notes: This supports Wired's 'top three'. Slany adds that GRIM had played 0.92% more games than OTFT (an error flagged by Abraham Heifets). Scaled for that, OTFT would have been 1st among non-group strategies. Slany argues GRIM's strong showing came from the STAR members defecting against everyone outside their group.

claims.claim: 2004 league 2 was the noisy variant with the same 223 strategies. Per Slany, the top three were again members of Ramchurn's STAR group. OTFT was 3rd among individuals, behind an individual strategy by Colm O'Riordan.
claims.quote: OTFT was placed as the second best non-group, individual strategy, placed third after three members of Ramchurn's STAR group and an individual strategy sent in by Colm O'Riordan
claims.source_title: Slany & Kienreich (2006/2007)
claims.notes: Read as written, the sentence is internally confusing: it says '2nd best non-group' but 'placed third after three STAR members and O'Riordan', which would make it 5th overall. Rogers et al. say 'the noisy IPD tournaments held at both events were won by a member of such a team, entered by the authors.'

claims.claim: In 2005 (CIG'05) a cap of 20 players per institution applied. Southampton entered one team using a [15,5] BCH error-correcting code with a TFT-default leader. In the noise-free tournament, three of the top four places went to different teams. In the noisy tournament, Southampton's leader won again, scoring 5% more than the second-placed competitor (averaged over five runs).
claims.quote: a fixed limit of 20 players per institution was established ... Within the noise free IPD tournament, three of the top four positions were occupied by representatives of different teams. However, within the noisy IPD tournament, our team leader again won with a clear advantage (averaged over five runs, it scored 5% more than the second placed competing player), despite using the tit-for-tat as a default strategy.
claims.source_title: Rogers et al., Theoretical Computer Science 377 (2007)
claims.notes: On whether collusion works under limited entries: under the 20-player cap it still won the noisy track. The paper credits error-correcting codes. Kendall's quoted 'around 20' (M05) is consistent with this.

claims.claim: Slany & Kienreich: the 2005 league 1 (standard rules) had 192 strategies and was won by their own 'CosaNostra Godfather', supported by 20 'Hitmen'. The 2005 league 4 allowed one strategy per team and had 50 strategies. It was won by APavlov (Jiawei Li), 1.2% ahead of OmegaTFT.
claims.quote: 2005 competition, league 1 (standard IPD rules, with 192 participating strategies) • CosaNostra Godfather was overall winner, with 20 CosaNostra Hitmen participating in the CosaNostra group strategy.
claims.source_title: Slany & Kienreich (2006/2007)
claims.notes: League 4 quote: 'Winner was the strategy APavlov sent in by Jia-Wei Li, outperforming our second placed OTFT by 1.2%.' So once entries were limited to one per team, colluding groups were excluded by design, and an adaptive Pavlov variant, not TFT, won. Counts for the 2005 noisy league were not found. The organizers' chapter was unreachable.

claims.claim: The Southampton paper is itself the main source on how much team size matters. In their own test population (18 classic strategies) with 10% noise, two team members win only 3.4% of the time without noise. In the alternative formats (ecological, remove-worst), a team of three or more still wins every competition.
claims.quote: with just two team members and no noise, a team player will win the tournament just 3.4% of the time. However, as the noise level increases, the performance of ... At a noise level of 1/5 the same team members win 70.2% of the time.
claims.source_title: Rogers et al., Theoretical Computer Science 377 (2007)
claims.notes: The quote is partial; the text between the ellipses is cut. This is a lab simulation, not the competition. Ecological-format claim: 'with three or more team players (one team leader and two or more team members), the team leader wins every competition.' The paper also notes that TFT 'performs relatively poorly' in their 18-strategy test population, beaten by Adaptive and Gradual.

claims.claim: Shalizi (bactra.org, Oct 2004) critique: the master/slave scheme is not evolutionarily stable. Slaves have no incentive to take part, and a mutant that defects against masters but plays TFT with everyone else would beat a slave.
claims.quote: the slave agents have, by construction, exactly no incentive to participate in the arrangement
claims.source_title: Cosma Shalizi, Three-Toed Sloth weblog, 14 Oct 2004
claims.notes: This is commentary, not data. Search snippets also attribute to a Freedom-to-Tinker (Princeton CITP) post the claim that 'Tit-for-Tat still scores higher than the average Southampton player'. That post was not opened.

claims.claim: The Axelrod-Python library's founding paper was published in the Journal of Open Research Software (2016, vol 4, e35, DOI 10.5334/jors.125), not PLoS ONE. Lead author is Vincent Knight, with 22 authors in total.
claims.quote: An open framework for the reproducible study of the iterated prisoner's dilemma.
claims.source_title: Knight et al., 'An Open Framework for the Reproducible Study of the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma', J. Open Research Software 4(1):e35 (arXiv v4, 20 Dec 2016)
claims.notes: The brief said PLoS ONE; that is wrong. The strategy count is inconsistent across versions and sections. arXiv v4 abstract: 'a growing collection of 136 strategies'. Body: '135 strategies are included'. Full-tournament figure: 129 strategies. The journal abstract, via a search snippet, says 139. Report it as 'about 130-140 at the time'.

claims.claim: Knight et al. 2016 findings: zero-determinant extortionate strategies win many individual matches but do poorly in overall ranking. Lookup-table and meta strategies (Looker Up, Meta Hunter) are 'generally cooperative yet still exploit naive strategies'.
claims.quote: extortionate strategies obtain a large number of wins: the number of times they outscore an opponent during a given match. However these do not perform particularly well from the overall tournament ranking point of view.
claims.source_title: Knight et al. 2016 (JORS)
claims.notes: The paper also reproduces Stewart & Plotkin's 19-strategy tournament. It gives no numeric rank for TFT in the text.

claims.claim: Harper et al. 2017 (PLoS ONE 12(12):e0188046, published 11 Dec 2017): 176 strategies (53 stochastic). Standard tournament: 200 turns. Noisy tournament: 5% chance of flipping each action. Each was repeated 50,000 times. Payoffs (R,P,T,S) = (3,1,5,0).
claims.quote: A total of 176 are included, of which 53 are stochastic. A standard tournament with 200 turns and a tournament with 5% noise is discussed. Due to the inherent stochasticity of these IPD tournaments, these tournaments were repeated 50000 times.
claims.source_title: Harper, Knight, Jones, Koutsovoulos, Glynatsi, Campbell, 'Reinforcement learning produces dominant strategies for the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma', PLoS ONE 2017
claims.notes: Training used evolutionary algorithms and particle swarm optimization (PSO), which the authors call 'reinforcement learning'. That is not RL in the modern deep-RL sense. The abstract says the strategies were trained 'against a corpus of over 170 distinct opponents'.

claims.claim: Harper 2017, standard tournament: the top 11 strategies by median payoff were all trained. Next came DBS (Desired Belief Strategy), then Winner12, Fool Me Once and Omega TFT. The worst rank EvolvedLookerUp2_2_2 reached in any tournament was 8th.
claims.quote: The top 11 performing strategies by median payoff are all strategies trained to maximize total payoff against a subset of the strategies (Table 2). The next strategy is Desired Belief Strategy (DBS)
claims.source_title: Harper et al. 2017, PLoS ONE
claims.notes: Also verbatim: 'the worst that the EvolvedLookerUp_2_2_2 ranks in any tournament is 8th.' The trained archetypes are lookup tables, Gambler, finite state machines (FSM), HMMs and neural networks (ANN). Discussion: 'In opposition to historical tournament results and community folklore, our results show that complex strategies can be effective for the IPD.'

claims.claim: Harper 2017 on TFT: over 50,000 standard tournaments TFT never wins a tournament and never wins a single match. It either draws through mutual cooperation or defects second. The paper gives no median rank for TFT in the text; its rank distribution appears only in Fig 9.
claims.quote: (We note that it never wins a tournament). Finally Fig 10 shows the number of opponents beaten in any given tournament: Tit For Tat does not win any match. (This is due to the fact that it will either draw with mutual cooperation or defect second).
claims.source_title: Harper et al. 2017, PLoS ONE
claims.notes: A numeric median rank for TFT was not extracted. It would have to be read from Fig 9 or the archived data (ref [31]).

claims.claim: Harper 2017, noisy (5%) tournament: DBS had the best median score, ahead of two noise-trained and three non-noise-trained strategies. DBS never ranked below 2nd and won 75% of the time. The two noise-trained strategies were top-3 95% of the time. Of the human-designed strategies, only DBS consistently performed well.
claims.quote: the DBS strategy never ranks lower than second and wins 75% of the time. The two strategies trained for noisy tournaments rank in the top three 95% of the time.
claims.source_title: Harper et al. 2017, PLoS ONE
claims.notes: Also verbatim: 'Of all the human-designed strategies in the library, only DBS consistently performs well, and it is substantially more complex than traditional tournament winners like TFT, OmegaTFT, and zero determinant strategies.' The noisy top-6 included PSO Gambler, yet it 'performs less well than' Spiteful TFT and OmegaTFT.

claims.claim: Harper 2017 still finds Axelrod's 'nice' property among the winners: the top strategies never defect first. The authors conclude that first impressions matter.
claims.quote: The best strategies are nice (never defecting first)
claims.source_title: Harper et al. 2017, PLoS ONE
claims.notes: The surrounding text says the top-3 strategies 'never defect first and learn to quickly punish poorer strategies'. So the winners are complex but still nice, which is a nuance for the article.

claims.claim: Glynatsi, Knight & Harper 2024 were published in PLoS Computational Biology 20(12):e1012644 on 26 Dec 2024, not Scientific Reports. The study used 195 strategies (Axelrod-Python v3.0.0) and four tournament types: standard, noisy, probabilistic ending, and noisy + probabilistic ending. The headline total is 45,600 tournaments (11,400 trials x 4).
claims.quote: We have run a total of 11400 trials of Algorithm 1. For each trial, we collect the results for four different tournaments, resulting in a total of 45600 (11400 × 4) tournament results.
claims.source_title: Glynatsi, Knight, Harper, 'Properties of winning Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma strategies', PLoS Comput Biol 2024
claims.notes: Internal inconsistency: Algorithm 1 loops 'for seed ∈ [0, 11420]', and Table 2 says 'based on 11420 unique tournaments' per type, but the text says 11,400 trials. Each trial randomizes the parameters: N ∈ [3,195] strategies, turns n ∈ [1,200], repetitions k ∈ [10,100], noise p_n ∈ [0,1], ending probability p_e ∈ [0,1]. Table 2 restricts the noisy and probabilistic-ending results to p ≤ 0.1, which leaves 1,151 and 1,139 tournaments.

claims.claim: Glynatsi 2024 headline: no single strategy excels everywhere. Successful strategies are 'nice, provocable and generous, a little envious, clever, and adapt to the environment', and they do best when their cooperation probability matches the population's aggregate cooperation.
claims.quote: We find that, while no single strategy consistently excels, successful strategies share key characteristics: they are nice, provocable and generous, a little envious, clever, and adapt to the environment.
claims.source_title: Glynatsi, Knight, Harper 2024, PLoS Comput Biol (Author summary)
claims.notes: Their refined rules, verbatim: 'Be a little bit envious; Be "nice" in non-noisy environments or when game lengths are longer; Reciprocate both cooperation and defection appropriately; Be provocable in tournaments with short matches, and generous in tournaments with noise; It's ok to be clever; Adapt to the environment; Adjust to the mean population cooperation'. So 'nice' holds conditionally, not universally. The authors say these findings 'challenge ... the advice to "not be clever" and "not be envious"'.

claims.claim: Glynatsi 2024 on envy: tournament winners show some extortionate (ZD-like) behavior, but less than many ZD strategies.
claims.quote: The winners of the tournaments considered in this work demonstrate envious behavior, but not to the extent observed in many ZDs.
claims.source_title: Glynatsi, Knight, Harper 2024, PLoS Comput Biol
claims.notes: Envy is measured by SSE distance to ZD behavior. ZD = zero-determinant (Press & Dyson 2012).

claims.claim: Glynatsi 2024: earlier tournament winners do not appear among the top performers against large opponent pools. In standard tournaments the top ranks are dominated by strategies trained with reinforcement learning (10 of the top 15 came from Harper 2017). In noisy tournaments (p_n ≤ 0.1), DBS ranks 1st with a median normalized rank of 0.
claims.quote: we show that the previous tournament winners are lacking against large enough opponent pools; they do not appear among the top-performing strategies anymore.
claims.source_title: Glynatsi, Knight, Harper 2024, PLoS Comput Biol
claims.notes: Also verbatim: 'In standard tournaments dominating strategies were those trained using reinforcement learning techniques. 10 out of the 15 top strategies were introduced in [23]' and 'For noisy tournaments DBS is the top ranked strategy with r̄ = 0, thus DBS won every tournament it participated in.'

claims.claim: Glynatsi 2024, TFT vs Gradual: TFT's normalized rank looks roughly normally distributed. Gradual has a lower median rank, so it does better than TFT, except in noisy and probabilistic-ending tournaments. TFT does best in probabilistic-ending tournaments, Gradual in standard ones.
claims.quote: Overall, Gradual achieves a lower median rank, signifying that it performs better than TFT except in the case of noisy and probabilistic ending tournaments (lower rank is better).
claims.source_title: Glynatsi, Knight, Harper 2024, PLoS Comput Biol
claims.notes: This is in the full random-parameter set. TFT's exact median normalized rank was not extracted; it is in Fig 2.

claims.claim: Current Axelrod-Python standing tournament (results for v4.13.1, pushed 30 Oct 2024): 236 strategies, 200 turns, 100 repetitions, seed 1. Standard tournament: TFT ranks 82nd of 236 (0-indexed rank 81), median score 2.602, 0 wins. Leader: EvolvedLookerUp2_2_2 (2.854). Gradual 15th; Grudger 40th; Cooperator 137th; Defector 232nd.
claims.source_title: Axelrod-Python-Tournament docs, std_summary.csv (GitHub Axelrod-Python/tournament, commit 'Add results for 4.13.1', 2024-10-30)
claims.notes: CSV URL: https://axelrod-tournament.readthedocs.io/en/latest/_downloads/06521e41d1988f718cb46ee467423437/std_summary.csv. Parameters come from run_std.py in the repo (turns=200, repetitions=100, seed=1). The CSV has 236 data rows, ranked 0-235. Top 10 are all trained: EvolvedLookerUp2_2_2, Evolved HMM 5, Evolved ANN 5, Evolved FSM 16, Evolved ANN, Evolved FSM 16 Noise 05, PSO Gambler 2_2_2, PSO Gambler 1_1_1, PSO Gambler Mem1, Evolved FSM 4.

claims.claim: Same standing tournament with 5% noise (run_noisy.py: noise=0.05, 200 turns, 100 repetitions): TFT ranks 61st of 236, median 2.154. Leader: Evolved ANN 5 Noise 05 (2.506), then DBS (2.458). Omega TFT 10th, Gradual 26th, Grudger 92nd, Defector 161st, Cooperator 206th.
claims.source_title: Axelrod-Python-Tournament docs, noisy_summary.csv (v4.13.1 results, 2024-10-30)
claims.notes: CSV URL: https://axelrod-tournament.readthedocs.io/en/latest/_downloads/9d6a34f750f60e5b526478e53eef813c/noisy_summary.csv. Under noise, TFT ranks relatively higher (61st vs 82nd), but it is still mid-table. Ranks here are 1-indexed; the CSV is 0-indexed. This is a single seeded run, not a distribution.

claims.claim: Rapoport, Seale & Colman 2015 (PLoS ONE 10(7):e0134128, published 30 Jul 2015) reanalyzed Axelrod's first-tournament score table as a two-stage tournament: all 756,756 ways of splitting the 15 programs into three groups of five, with group winners meeting in a final round-robin. TFT won only 11.0% of these; T&C (Tideman & Chieruzzi) won 30.0% and S&R (Stein & Rapoport) 24.8%. TFT won the preliminary stage most often (42.1%).
claims.quote: Table 3 shows that Program 2 (T&C) won 30.0% of the tournaments, Program 6 (S&R) came second with 24.8%, whereas Program 1 (TFT) only won 11.0%.
claims.source_title: Rapoport, Seale, Colman, 'Is Tit-for-Tat the Answer? On the Conclusions Drawn from Axelrod's Tournaments', PLoS ONE 2015
claims.notes: Program full names (Tideman & Chieruzzi, Stein & Rapoport) are from Axelrod 1980 entrant list, not this paper's abbreviations — verify. This is a recomputation from Axelrod's published pairwise score table, not new play. The top eight ('nice') programs took 99.7% of wins. In a round-robin of only the top-8 nice programs, 'TFT was one of the four programs that tied for the lowest ranking'. The authors attribute TFT's original win largely to two 'kingmakers' (DOWNING and GRAASKAMP).

claims.claim: Rapoport et al. 2015 on scoring criterion: ranked by number of pairwise wins, TFT comes last in Axelrod's first tournament (zero wins). The points ranking and the wins ranking are uncorrelated (Spearman ρ = −.103). In the 2004 Kendall competition (223 programs) the correlation is ρ = −.45 (p < 0.001).
claims.quote: TFT did not score even a single win—by its nature, it can never outscore its co-player—and was ranked last. The Spearman rank correlation between the two rankings turns out to be ρ = −.103.
claims.source_title: Rapoport, Seale, Colman 2015, PLoS ONE
claims.notes: Discrepancy: RSC describe the 2004 tournament as having 'incorporated random noise', while Slany describes league 1 as 'standard IPD rules' and league 2 as the noisy variant. It is unclear which league's table RSC used (their ref [21], an online table). Abstract conclusion: TFT's efficacy 'is contingent on the design of the tournament, the criterion used to determine success, and the particular values chosen for the Prisoner's Dilemma payoff matrix'. The payoff-matrix argument is a conjecture citing Kretz, not a new simulation.

claims.claim: Beaufils, Delahaye & Mathieu introduced the 'Gradual' strategy at Artificial Life V (Nara, 16-18 May 1996; MIT Press, pp. 202-209) and claimed it outperforms TFT. Gradual is a TFT variant whose retaliation grows with each defection, followed by two cooperative 'calming' moves.
claims.source_title: Beaufils, Delahaye, Mathieu, 'Our Meeting With Gradual: A Good Strategy For The Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma', Artificial Life V (1996)
claims.notes: The PDF server refused the connection (ECONNREFUSED), so the paper was not read. The abstract claim comes from a search snippet. The mechanism description is backed by Rogers et al. 2007 Table A.1 ('Modified tit-for-tat strategy that use progressively longer sequences...'). Some citations date it 1997. Independent later confirmation that Gradual beats TFT: M25 (Glynatsi 2024, standard tournaments) and M26 (Gradual 15th vs TFT 82nd).

open_questions: Is the Southampton 2004 count 60 (Wired) or 112 (Rogers et al. 2007: 4 teams x 28; Slany: STAR group 112)? The papers agree on 112. The organizers' chapter (Chong/Humble/Kendall/Li/Yao, '20 Years On' ch.1) returned 403 and should be checked for the official count.
Which 2004 league does Rogers' '13% more than the second placed competing player' refer to? It does not match Slany's league-1 table (+16.3% over GRIM, +5.8% over StarS).

Was the 2004 'main' tournament noisy? Southampton's press release and RSC 2015 emphasize noise. Slany describes league 1 as standard and league 2 as noisy. Wired's '223 entries' and 'top three' fit league 1.
Who said 'we would have won with around 20'? The repost suggests Kendall, but the pronoun 'we' is odd for an organizer. Verify against the original Wired text, which wired.com blocked.

Not found: 2005 CIG entry counts for the noisy league and leagues 2-3 (Slany gives league 1 = 192 and league 4 = 50 only). The noise probability used in 2004/2005 was also not found; Rogers' simulations used 1/10, but that is their own setting.
TFT's median rank across Harper 2017's 50,000 tournaments is only in Fig 9 and was not extracted numerically. The same goes for TFT's median normalized rank in Glynatsi 2024 (Fig 2).
Beaufils et al. 1996 Gradual paper (cristal.univ-lille.fr) was unreachable; its experimental numbers (pool size, ranks vs TFT) are unverified.

Unreached: the Southampton ECS news item 612 (403), the prisoners-dilemma.com official site via Wayback (archive offline / blocked), and the Freedom-to-Tinker post claiming TFT out-scored the average Southampton player.
